# Chapter 9: Common Design Patterns — 9.1–9.3

Rules that no analyzer enforces (judgment), and CONSIDER rules that analyzers only suggest. Open the examples file for the explanation and code the book gives with each rule.

## 9.1.3 Aggregate Component Guidelines

- **FDG9001** CONSIDER providing aggregate components for commonly used feature areas. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9001
- **FDG9002** DO model high-level concepts (physical objects) rather than system-level tasks with aggregate components. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9002
- **FDG9003** DO increase the visibility of aggregate components by giving them names that correspond to well-known entities of the system, such as `MessageQueue`, `Process`, or `EventLog`. (not in test projects)
- **FDG9004** DO design aggregate components so they can be used after very simple initialization. If some initialization is necessary, the exception resulting from not having the component initialized should clearly explain what needs to be done. (not in test projects)
- **FDG9005** DO NOT require the users of aggregate components to explicitly instantiate multiple objects in a single scenario. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9005
- **FDG9006** DO make sure aggregate components support the Create–Set–Call usage pattern, where developers expect to be able to implement most scenarios by instantiating the component, setting its properties, and calling simple methods. (not in test projects)
- **FDG9007** DO provide a default or a very simple constructor for all aggregate components. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9007
- **FDG9008** DO provide properties with getters and setters corresponding to all parameters of aggregate component constructors. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9008
- **FDG9009** DO use events instead of delegate-based APIs in aggregate components. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9009
- **FDG9010** DO use events in aggregate components instead of virtual members that need to be overridden. (not in test projects)
- **FDG9011** DO NOT require users of aggregate components to inherit, override methods, or implement any interfaces in common scenarios. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9011
- **FDG9012** DO NOT require users of aggregate components to do anything besides writing code in common scenarios. For example, users should not have to configure components in the configuration file, generate any resource files, and so on. (not in test projects)
- **FDG9013** CONSIDER making changes to aggregate components’ modes automatic. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9013
- **FDG9014** DO NOT design factored types that have modes. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9014
- **FDG9015** CONSIDER integrating your aggregate components with Visual Studio designers. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9015
- **FDG9016** CONSIDER separating aggregate components and factored types into different assemblies. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9016
- **FDG9017** CONSIDER exposing access to internal factored types of an aggregate component. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9017

## 9.2.1 Choosing Between the Async Patterns

- **FDG9018** DO implement new asynchronous API using the Task-Based Async Pattern. (not in test projects)
- **FDG9019** CONSIDER upgrading a Classic Async Pattern or Event-Based Async Pattern API to the Task-Based Async Pattern. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9019

## 9.2.2 Task-Based Async Pattern

- **FDG9021** CONSIDER adding synchronous variants of Async methods. (library only) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9021
- **FDG9024** CONSIDER keeping the `CancellationToken` as the last parameter, for better alignment with a synchronous version of the method. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9024
- **FDG9025** CONSIDER accepting a `CancellationToken` in long-running or blocking synchronous methods. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9025
- **FDG9026** DO NOT return Tasks for long-running synchronous methods. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9026

## 9.2.3 Async Method Return Types

- **FDG9030** DO use (non-generic) `Task` as the preferred return type for an asynchronous method that does not produce a value. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9030
- **FDG9031** DO use `Task<TResult>` as the preferred return type for an asynchronous method that produces a value. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9031
- **FDG9032** CONSIDER returning `ValueTask<TResult>` from an asynchronous method when the method commonly completes synchronously. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9032

## 9.2.4 Making an Async Variant of an Existing Synchronous Method

- **FDG9034** DO convert the signature as needed to remove any `ref` or `out` parameters from an asynchronous method. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9034
- **FDG9035** CONSIDER replacing synchronous callbacks with asynchronous callbacks in the Async method, or accepting both via overloading. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9035

## 9.2.5.5 Exceptions from Async Methods

- **FDG9044** DO throw execution error exceptions via the Task-like value returned from an Async method. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9044

## 9.2.10 IAsyncEnumerable&lt;T>

- **FDG9046** DO add the `[EnumeratorCancellation]` attribute to the `CancellationToken` parameter of an `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` method using `yield return`. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9046

## 9.3 Dependency Properties

- **FDG9051** DO provide properties as dependency properties if you need the properties to support WPF features such as styling, triggers, data binding, animations, dynamic resources, and inheritance. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9051

## 9.3.1 Dependency Property Design

- **FDG9058** DO NOT use dependency properties to store secure data. Even private dependency properties can be accessed publicly. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9058

## 9.3.3 Dependency Property Validation

- **FDG9059** DO NOT put dependency property validation logic in the property’s accessors. Instead, pass a validation callback to `DependencyProperty.Register` method. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9059

## 9.3.4 Dependency Property Change Notifications

- **FDG9060** DO NOT implement change notification logic in dependency property accessors. Dependency properties have a built-in change notifications feature that is used by supplying a change notification callback to the `PropertyMetadata`. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9060

## 9.3.5 Dependency Property Value Coercion

- **FDG9061** DO NOT implement coercion logic in dependency property accessors. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch09-patterns-aggregate-async.md#fdg9061
